archetype.name: Game Manager (short-area backup)
archetype.definition: A 6-foot-6 pocket backup who lives on throws inside 10 air yards, rarely runs, and has not yet shown he can make the defense pay vertically when he is asked to start.

report.headline: A checkdown backup whose short game can't outrun the sacks and dead deep shots
report.take:
Tanner McKee is a fourth-year, sixth-round backup who has now had the most extended run of his career: three games in Weeks 6 through 8, every snap in each, two official starts, and an 0-3 record with no covers. He plays like a quarterback trying not to lose the game. His average throw lands 2.84 yards short of the sticks, his aggressiveness fell from 22.2% in Week 6 to 8.8% by Week 8, and most of his attempts go underneath. That approach keeps the interception rate tolerable at 1.8%, below the league's 2.5%. It also caps the offense: 5.6 yards per attempt ranks 47th of 54 qualifiers, and his dropbacks cost his team -16.8 EPA in total.

The season splits cleanly by depth. Under 10 air yards he completes 72.1% with a slightly positive CPOE (+1.3) and roughly neutral EPA. That is real, functional quarterbacking. At 10-plus he completes 35.7%, and on throws of 20-plus he is 0-for-8 with an interception and -9.2 EPA. Those eight throws alone wipe out everything the short game built. Screens and throws behind the line have also been a drain (-0.26 EPA a play), and his backfield targets, Elijah Mitchell above all at -0.403 per target, have produced little.

The passing yardage hides how weak this has been. He averages 212.7 a game, above the 190.1 league average and good for 22nd, but that is volume from a team that trailed in every game. His best-looking numbers come while trailing by nine or more: 70.7% completions and a +6.7 CPOE against defenses sitting back. In one-score games, where the outcome was still in play, his success rate drops to 32.9% and his CPOE to -7.5. The sacks are the other hidden cost. He takes them at 8.1%, and a pressure-to-sack rate of 31.3% is high for someone with an ordinary 2.65-second release and almost no scrambling (5 scrambles on 129 dropbacks). That looks like a quarterback without answers when the first read is covered, not one extending plays to create something.

The career record agrees. His bad-throw rate ranked near the bottom of the league in 2024 and 2025 one-game cameos and sits 37th of 42 this year at 17.5%. That is a trait, not a slump. The bright 2024 cameo (+0.31 EPA a play, four touchdowns) is one game. The 2026 body of work is three times larger and says he is a replacement-level starter on an offense that ranks 29th in EPA. He is listed as QB2 behind an unnamed starter, Joe Milton III started Week 9, and McKee was limited and questionable at that week's practice. Any rest-of-season value is contingent and modest.

strengths.title: Accurate and efficient underneath
strengths.body: Inside 10 air yards he completes 72.1% with a positive CPOE, and the 0-9 range has added EPA at +0.083 a play. Throwing on time to short, defined reads is the reason his interception rate stays reasonable. This is the stable part of his game: it fits his size, his release and a conservative plan, and it should hold.

strengths.title: Middle of the field works
strengths.body: When he works between the numbers, the results flip: +0.359 EPA a play over the middle and +0.222 on intermediate throws, against negative EPA to both sidelines. Middle throws use his height and let him read one defender instead of fitting balls outside. Both samples are around 20 attempts, so this is a hint, not a fact. It is still the most useful clue for how an offense should call plays for him.

strengths.title: Limits the interceptions
strengths.body: His 1.8% interception rate ranks 19th of 54 and sits under the league average. That is a direct product of his short-throw diet. The cost is explosiveness, but for a backup asked to keep a struggling offense on schedule, avoiding the turnover is the job.

concerns.title: No vertical answer at all
concerns.body: Downfield he is 0-for-8 on 20-plus-yard throws for -9.2 EPA, and his completion rate on all 10-plus throws is 35.7%. That reflects the career-long bad-throw problem more than bad luck. Defenses can squat on the short game because the deep threat is not credible. Eight deep attempts is a small sample, but the 10-plus split and the bad-throw history point the same way.

concerns.title: Pressure turns into sacks
concerns.body: He converts 31.3% of pressures into sacks and was sacked five times at Washington in Week 8, along with a lost fumble. His release is not long and he barely scrambles, so the sacks are not the price of extending plays. They look like hesitation when the first read is gone. That is the more worrying kind of sack problem, and it gets worse against good pass rushes.

concerns.title: Fades when games are close
concerns.body: In one-score situations his success rate is 32.9% with a -7.5 CPOE. His third-down conversion rate is 28.6% while facing 9.4 yards to go on average. The prettier numbers come in comeback mode against soft coverage. The offense around him (31st in success rate) and two missing wideouts explain some of this, but not the accuracy drop.

trend.note: Steady in the worst sense: 215, 211 and 212 passing yards, negative EPA every week, and the Week 7 game (-2.3) was the only near-neutral outing. Aggressiveness shrank each week and Week 8 brought five sacks and his worst EPA game (-8.8), so if anything the trend leans down.

nextGame.headline: Sack-happy Steelers front meets a QB who may not even start
nextGame.body:
If McKee plays, Pittsburgh is a poor fit for him. The Steelers are 7th in sack rate and 7th against the run, so offenses pass on them more than usual (5th-strongest pass funnel), and he would likely face a heavy dropback load behind a line that let him get sacked five times in Week 8. Their weakness is deep: they rank 23rd in deep-pass EPA allowed, but he has completed none of his eight deep attempts. Underneath, where he is comfortable, they are a little better than average (12th). The one inviting spot is the tight end, where Pittsburgh ranks 30th in EPA allowed to the TE1. With the Eagles 4.5-point home underdogs and a 38.5 total, the Book expects a low-scoring game the Steelers control.

Availability frames everything. McKee is listed as QB2 and was limited and questionable at his last practice report, and Joe Milton III started Week 9, so he may not take a snap. If he does, DeVonta Smith (hamstring) and Dontayvion Wicks (ankle) are both out, with return estimates of game day. Without them his receiving corps is thin: Makai Lemon, his most productive target, would face a defense that ranks 3rd against WR1s. Pittsburgh hopes to get receivers Michael Pittman Jr. and Roman Wilson back from IR, which would help the Steelers sustain drives against an Eagles defense ranked 27th, while likely losing guard Mason McCormick. The early forecast shows gusts near 29 mph and rain showers; that is hedged at five days out, but it would push both teams toward a ground game the Eagles struggle to run.

keyMatchups.title: Pittsburgh's pass rush vs his sack rate
keyMatchups.body: A top-10 sack defense against a quarterback who turns nearly a third of pressures into sacks is the central problem. Expect drive-killing negative plays unless the plan is almost entirely quick game.

keyMatchups.title: Goedert against a soft TE defense
keyMatchups.body: Pittsburgh has allowed +0.45 EPA a play to tight ends, 30th in the league. Goedert has been positive on McKee's targets, and the middle of the field is where McKee is best, so this is the cleanest path to efficient plays.

keyMatchups.title: Lemon vs a stingy WR1 defense
keyMatchups.body: With Smith and Wicks out, Lemon is the de facto top receiver against a defense ranked 3rd in EPA allowed to WR1s. McKee's best target faces Pittsburgh's best coverage.

nextGame.watch: Whether McKee is named the starter at all. If he is, watch how many of his throws travel 10+ air yards against a defense that leaks deep.

restOfSeason.body:
If he gets more starts, expect the same shape: plenty of short completions, passing yards around 185 to 235 a game when trailing, and few touchdowns. His 1.8% TD rate sits well below the league's 4.0%, and his two scores came on just six red-zone plays, which is noise in both directions. Some things should hold: the conservative throw profile, the high sack rate and the career-long bad-throw problem. One thing should improve somewhat: 0-for-8 deep is unlikely to stay a total zero. The interception rate could drift up toward league average if he ever starts pushing the ball more.

The ceiling is set by context as much as by him. He is the QB2 on an offense ranked 29th, with a defense ranked 27th forcing comeback scripts. Smith's and Wicks' return would give him real targets beyond Lemon and Goedert. The bigger variable is whether he plays at all: on the dossier he is a spot starter whose value appears only if the quarterbacks ahead of him are unavailable.

confidence.note: Three games, two starts, QB2 on the depth chart with an injury tag.
